For an odd prime $p$, let $\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ and define
$a*b=2b-a$. Then $(\mathbb F_p,*)$ is a quandle.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

derivations.claim: For fixed $b\in\mathbb F_p$, define $R_b(a)=a*b=2b-a$. Then $R_b(R_b(a))=2b-(2b-a)=a$, so $R_b^{-1}=R_b$. Also $a*a=2a-a=a$. Thus both the forward and reverse crossing rules use the same involution, and an arc's color is uniquely recoverable across one underpass.

In an R1 disk, the coloring relation on the kinked side is either $y=x*x$ or $x=y*x$, where $x$ is the unchanged boundary color and $y$ is the color of the new interior underarc. In the first case $y=x$ by idempotency; in the second, $R_x(y)=x$ has the unique solution $y=R_x(x)=x$ because $R_x$ is bijective. Deleting the kink is the inverse restriction map. The two formulas cover both strand directions because the inverse operation equals the operation by step 1.1.

In an R2 disk, fix the color $b$ of the strand passing over the other strand and the incoming underarc color $a$. The first crossing changes the underarc color to $R_b(a)$, and the second changes it by $R_b^{-1}$; their composition is $R_b^{-1}(R_b(a))=a$. Therefore every boundary coloring extends uniquely across the two-crossing side, and the reverse R2 move gives the inverse bijection. Other orientation variants replace one of these maps by its inverse, which is the same map by step 1.1.

For a braid-like R3 orientation, start with boundary colors $a,b,c$. Propagating through the two sides gives respectively $(c,b*c,(a*b)*c)$ and $(c,b*c,(a*c)*(b*c))$. The last coordinates agree by right self-distributivity in [F2], so every boundary coloring on either side has a unique matching extension on the other. Reversing a crossing replaces a right translation by its inverse; step 1.1 makes that the same map, and relabeling the three strands gives every height-order and orientation variant in [F3].

If $D$ is empty, its unique empty coloring is carried to itself by planar isotopy, and no Reidemeister move is supported on the empty diagram. If $D$ is nonempty, planar isotopy carries every arc and local crossing relation bijectively to its image, while steps 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 give explicit coloring bijections for every local move. Composing the finitely many bijections along any finite move sequence preserves the coloring count. These constructions act on finite arc labels and use no choice principle.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram: a projection of a finite union of oriented circles with finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and one overpassing branch specified at each double point. Let $c(D)$ be its number of crossings and $m(D)$ its number of components. An arc is a connected strand segment cut at each undercrossing; each component with no undercrossings contributes one closed arc. Write $a(D)$ for the number of arcs. If $q(D)$ components have no undercrossings, then $a(D)=c(D)+q(D)$ and $0\le q(D)\le m(D)$.

A supplied finite code for $D$ has code length $L$, the total number of bits in that literal code, including its tags, signs, labels, and separators. The length depends on the chosen encoding. In particular, for one of the tagged Gauss, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite, or oriented planar-diagram formats, $L$ is the bit length of the supplied valid code in that format. The procedures in this page take typed mathematical diagrams or valid codes as stated; no string parser or malformed-code behavior is included in any operation count.

For an integer $z$, define its signed-magnitude bit length by $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(0)=1$ and $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil$ for $z\ne0$. For a Laurent polynomial $P(A)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}z_jA^j$ with finite support, define its coefficient-bit size as $0$ if $P=0$, and otherwise as $\max_{j:z_j\ne0}\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z_j)$. Its absolute Laurent degree is $\max_{j:z_j\ne0}|j|$, with value $0$ for $P=0$. For a prime $p$, elements of $\mathbb F_p$ are represented exactly by residues $0,\ldots,p-1$, and their representation uses $\lceil\log_2p\rceil$ bits.

An exact output is the complete integer, finite list, or Laurent polynomial with its integer coefficients and exponents. A floating-point approximation is not an exact output. A field-operation count treats each addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero element, and equality test in $\mathbb F_p$ as one operation; this convention does not assert that these operations have constant bit cost as $p$ varies.

The input is a nonempty unoriented regular link diagram $D$: a finite immersed
planar projection of one or more circles with finitely many transverse double
points, no triple points, and over/under data at each double point. Let $C(D)$
be its finite crossing set. At each crossing take the local chart in which the
over-strand runs southwest to northeast and is drawn continuously over the
under-strand, which runs northwest to southeast with a gap at the intersection.
The A-smoothing joins the two left endpoints and the two right endpoints, with
weight $A$; the B-smoothing joins the two top endpoints and the two bottom
endpoints, with weight $A^{-1}$. These labels are transported with
orientation-preserving changes of local coordinates. Put
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. The output is the Laurent polynomial $\langle D\rangle$.

1. Set an accumulator $p:=0$ in $\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$.
2. For each function $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$, smooth every crossing according to
   $S$, obtaining a crossingless diagram with $|S|$ circles. Count the A- and
   B-smoothings as $a(S)$ and $b(S)$, and replace
   $$p\quad\text{by}\quad p+A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}.$$
3. Return $p$ after all states have been processed.

The input is a mathematical diagram object, not a serialized string. The
procedure specifies no parsing or malformed-string rejection behavior. Since
the diagram has at least one component, every complete smoothing has
$|S|\ge1$ and every exponent of $\delta$ is nonnegative.

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$ be a typed nonempty unoriented regular
link diagram with finite crossing set $C(D)$. At each crossing use the chart
with the over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins the left endpoints and the
right endpoints with weight $A$, while B joins the top endpoints and bottom
endpoints with weight $A^{-1}$. The Kauffman bracket state-sum algorithm
terminates after exactly $2^{|C(D)|}$ state visits and returns
$$\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1},$$
where $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count the two smoothing types and $|S|$ counts the
circles in the smoothed diagram. The algorithm takes a mathematical diagram
as input and makes no claim about parsing strings or rejecting malformed
encodings.

derivations.claim: The state set has exactly $2^c$ elements by [F3]. A complete smoothing starts with $m$ circles. At each crossing the four local endpoints lie on one or two current circles, and either smoothing reconnects them into one or two circles. Thus the circle count increases by at most one at each of the $c$ smoothings. Every state has $1\le |S|\le m+c$.

For a fixed state, put $r=|S|-1$, so $0\le r\le m+c-1$. The binomial theorem gives $\delta^r=(-1)^r\sum_{k=0}^r\binom{r}{k}A^{2r-4k}$. These exponents are distinct, so its coefficient l1 norm is $\sum_{k=0}^r\binom{r}{k}=2^r$; multiplication by the monomial $A^{a(S)-b(S)}$ only shifts the exponents.

Since $a(S)+b(S)=c$, one has $|a(S)-b(S)|\le c$. The exponents in $\delta^r$ lie between $-2r$ and $2r$. Using $r\le m+c-1$, every exponent in every state term, and thus in the sum, has absolute value at most $c+2(m+c-1)=3c+2m-2$.

Put $q=c+m+1\ge2$. Represent a crossing endpoint by an integer from $1$ to $4c$, grouped into four successive ports at each crossing, and write $\alpha$ for the supplied edge-pairing involution. For a state, let $\beta$ pair the two left and two right ports for A, or the two top and two bottom ports for B. The multigraph on the $4c$ endpoints with one $\alpha$-edge and one $\beta$-edge at every vertex is two-regular, allowing parallel edges. Each connected component follows one smoothed circle, and the $u$ supplied crossingless components add $u$ further circles. Thus a traversal marking a vertex when first queued computes $|S|$ exactly. The same traversal, with the opposite ports paired instead of smoothing ports, computes the original component count $m$; perform it once initially and then compute $q$ for allocation. Use binary counters and linear scans for all table and mark lookups: there are $O(q)$ endpoint visits, each using a bounded number of scans of $O(q)$ records with $O(\log q)$ index bits. Even with a work-tape queue or stack scanned linearly, each visit costs $O(q^2)$ bit steps, so tracing costs $O(q^3)$. Computing $a(S)-b(S)$ and adding $u$ use counters of $O(\log q)$ bits and fit this bound. Enumerate the states with a $c$-bit binary counter, making exactly $2^c$ visits; the $c=0$ case is one empty mask with $|S|=u=m$. Reading the stated input takes $O(q\log q)$ steps and is included.

Summing over all $2^c$ states, the l1 norm of the final coefficient sequence is at most the sum of the state-term l1 norms, hence at most $2^c2^{m+c-1}=2^{m+2c-1}$. Every individual coefficient therefore has absolute value at most $2^{m+2c-1}$.

Let $M=m+2c\ge1$. By step 3.1, a nonzero coefficient $z_j$ satisfies $|z_j|\le2^{M-1}$, so $|z_j|+1\le2^M$ and $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z_j)=1+\lceil\log_2(|z_j|+1)\rceil\le M+1=m+2c+1$. The support lies in at most $6c+4m-3$ integer exponents by step 2.2, so storing the exact polynomial as a dense coefficient array takes $O((c+m)^2)$ bits. For a knot, $m=1$, giving degree at most $3c$ and coefficient-bit size at most $2c+2$, both linear in $c+1$.

Use coefficient slots for every exponent from $-3q$ to $3q$, padded with zeros, and use $2q+3$ bits per signed-magnitude slot, plus $O(\log q)$-bit position counters. These arrays have $O(q^2)$ tape cells. Every partial accumulator, not just the final sum, has coefficient l1 norm at most $2^c2^{m+c-1}$: apply the triangle inequality in step 3.1 to the subset of states already processed. Hence its coefficients fit the chosen width, since $m+2c-1<2q$. For one state compute $r=|S|-1$ and start with the array for $P_0=1$. For $k=0,\ldots,r-1$, form a new array by the exact recurrence $(P_{k+1})_j=-(P_k)_{j-2}-(P_k)_{j+2}$, reading absent coefficients as zero. This is multiplication by $\delta$, so $P_r=\delta^r$. All intermediate powers have degree at most $2r<2q$ and l1 norm at most $2^r\le2^{m+c-1}$, so they too fit the arrays and widths.

Here is a direct tape bound without unit-cost access or integer arithmetic. To retrieve or write a coefficient, scan an entire array of $O(q)$ slots of $O(q)$ bits, advancing a binary slot counter and comparing it with the desired index. The counter work is $O(q\log q)$ and the scanned data have $O(q^2)$ bits, so one lookup or write costs $O(q^2)$ bit steps. Addition or subtraction of two signed integers in these slots is performed by sign comparison, a linear magnitude comparison, and the usual binary carry or borrow scan, costing $O(q)$ steps; the extra carry bit fits the reserved width. For each of the $O(q)$ destination coefficients in the recurrence of step 4.2, make at most two source lookups, one such addition, and one destination write. A multiplication by $\delta$ therefore costs $O(q^3)$ steps. There are $r<q$ repetitions, giving $O(q^4)$ work. Shift this state polynomial by $a(S)-b(S)$ and add it to the accumulator coefficient by coefficient using the same linear scans; the state shift has magnitude at most $c$, its support stays inside the slots by step 2.2, and this accumulation costs $O(q^3)$. Clearing arrays, moving the state counter, and loop-index bookkeeping are bounded by the same charges.

Summing the per-state bounds in steps 2.3, 4.2, and 5.1 over exactly $2^c$ visits gives $O(2^cq^4)$ bit steps. The initial component-count traversal costs $O(q^3)$ by step 2.3; coefficient-array initialization and writing the dense exact output cost $O(q^2)$. These are absorbed because $2^c\ge1$ and $q\ge2$. The loop tracing and arithmetic realize exactly the state terms in [F2], so [F3] identifies the result with the bracket. When $c=0$, the single state computes $\delta^{m-1}$ with the same bound; when $m=1$, $q=c+2$ gives $O(2^c(c+1)^4)$. All choices and operations are finite. The bit-cost argument concerns only the specified indexed table and elementary binary operations, so it makes no claim about parsing arbitrary code strings of length $L$ or the cost of an unspecified arithmetic library.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

Input a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings,
fixed finite orderings of its arcs and crossings, and an odd prime $p$. The algorithm returns the full set
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$ of assignments of residues in $\mathbb F_p$ to the
arcs satisfying the Fox crossing equations, together with
$|\operatorname{Col}_p(D)|$.

1. Create one variable $x_j$ for each arc in the supplied order, and process
   crossings in the supplied order.
2. At each crossing with overarc $o$ and the two underarcs $i$ and $j$, append
   the homogeneous linear equation $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.
   At a crossing, add the coefficients of any repeated arc in that row.
3. Set the next pivot-row index to $r=1$ and process columns from left to
   right. If $r>c$, mark this and every remaining column free and stop. If
   $r\le c$, search rows $r,\ldots,c$ in order for the first nonzero entry in
   the current column. If none exists, mark this column free and continue
   without changing $r$. Otherwise swap the selected row into row $r$, divide
   row $r$ by its nonzero entry in this column, and add multiples of row $r$
   to every other row to clear this column. Record this column as a pivot
   column with pivot row $r$, then increase $r$ by one. After the scan, every
   column not recorded as a pivot column is free.
4. List the free columns in increasing order and enumerate every tuple in
   $\mathbb F_p^f$ in lexicographic order using the residue representatives
   $0,\ldots,p-1$, where $f$ is the number of free columns. If $f=0$, process
   the empty tuple once. For each tuple, assign its coordinates to the free
   variables. For each pivot row, set its pivot variable equal to the negative
   of the sum of the row's free-column coefficients times those assigned free
   variables. Append the resulting assignment in the supplied arc order.
   Return all appended assignments and their number.

For every odd prime $p$ and every finite regular oriented link diagram $D$,
the algorithm in the Definition terminates and returns exactly
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$. If its reduced system has $f$ free variables, it
returns $p^f$ colorings. It uses at most $a$ pivot steps and at most $ca$
row-entry elimination scans for a diagram with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. A Fox $p$-coloring of a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ assigns an element of $\mathbb F_p$ to each arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing, where $x_o$ is the overarc color and $x_i,x_j$ are the two underarc colors. If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move of type R1, R2, or R3, restriction outside the move disk gives a bijection from the Fox $p$-colorings of $D$ to those of $D'$. Consequently the number of Fox $p$-colorings is unchanged along every finite sequence of such moves. The local bijections use no choice principle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

derivations.claim: The linking scan performs one visit per element of the finite crossing list by [F2]. On a two-component input each visit makes at most one component-membership test and, for a mixed crossing, one integer addition, so there are at most $c$ tests and $c$ additions after the constant-size component-count check. Each added term is $+1$ or $-1$, hence the absolute value of the sum is at most $c$ and the returned half-sum has absolute value at most $c/2$. The result is an integer and is the diagram's linking number by [F3] and [F4].

For each of the $c$ crossings, [F5] contributes three coefficients to a row. If arc labels repeat, combining at most three contributions requires at most two field additions for that row, so setup uses at most $2c$ additions; initializing the dense $c\times a$ matrix writes $ca$ zeros. There are $a$ columns, and each pivot search checks at most $c$ rows, for at most $ca$ entry tests.

Let $r$ be the number of pivots, so $r\le\min(c,a)$ and $f=a-r$. Normalizing each pivot row divides at most $a$ entries by its nonzero pivot, for at most $ra$ divisions. Clearing a pivot column from each of at most $c-1$ other rows updates at most $a$ entries, with at most one multiplication and one addition per entry. The row-reduction arithmetic count is therefore at most $ra+2r(c-1)a$. These loops are finite because there are at most $a$ columns and $c$ rows.

There are exactly $p^f$ assignments to the $f$ free variables by [F6]. For each assignment, each of the $a-f$ pivot variables is a linear combination of at most $f$ free variables; computing it uses at most $f$ multiplications and $f$ additions/subtractions, including the final negation. Writing the full solution uses $a$ output entries. Thus listing every coloring uses at most $p^f(2f(a-f)+a)$ field arithmetic and output-write operations. The loop is finite, including $f=0$, when there is one solution and only the $a$ entries are written.

For $f=0$, the count is $1$ without multiplication. For $f\ge1$, binary repeated squaring computes $p^f$ with at most $2\lceil\log_2(f+1)\rceil$ integer multiplications. Since $f\le a$, the magnitude bit length is at most $f\lceil\log_2p\rceil+1$. This count-only postprocessing does not enumerate the solution set and does not change the full-list cost in step 3.1.

The diagram-by-diagram scan, matrix construction, row reduction, and finite solution enumeration above use no choice principle. By [F7], the Fox coloring count is preserved along every finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves; by [A1] and [F8], ambient-isotopic oriented links admit such a sequence. By [F4], the linking-number half-sum has the same move invariance. Thus ACω is used only for the ambient-isotopy interpretations, not for any finite operation count.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $c(D)$ be its number of crossings and $m(D)$ its number of components. An arc is a connected strand segment cut at each undercrossing; each component with no undercrossings contributes one closed arc. Write $a(D)$ for the number of arcs. If $q(D)$ components have no undercrossings, then $a(D)=c(D)+q(D)$ and $0\le q(D)\le m(D)$.

A supplied finite code for $D$ has code length $L$, the total number of bits in that literal code, including its tags, signs, labels, and separators. The length depends on the chosen encoding. In particular, for one of the tagged Gauss, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite, or oriented planar-diagram formats, $L$ is the bit length of the supplied valid code in that format. The procedures in this page take typed mathematical diagrams or valid codes as stated; no string parser or malformed-code behavior is included in any operation count.

For an integer $z$, define its signed-magnitude bit length by $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(0)=1$ and $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil$ for $z\ne0$. For a Laurent polynomial $P(A)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}z_jA^j$ with finite support, define its coefficient-bit size as $0$ if $P=0$, and otherwise as $\max_{j:z_j\ne0}\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z_j)$. over-strand runs southwest to northeast and is drawn continuously over the
under-strand, which runs northwest to southeast with a gap at the intersection.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

**Input:** Two valid normalized oriented planar-diagram codes $C_0,C_1$ for connected one-component knot diagrams.

**Output:** The algorithm returns Found(path) only if it has a finite sequence of code classes from $C_0$ to $C_1$, with a finite local-move certificate for each adjacent pair. It has no negative-output branch. It may run forever if the target code class is never reached.

**Instructions:**

1. Validate both input codes using the planar-code validation procedure. If either is invalid, return that first invalid-code result. For each valid code, form its canonical representative by checking all bijections of its finite crossing labels and edge labels, recomputing the prescribed edge normalization, and selecting the lexicographically least resulting code.
2. Set the initial frontier to the singleton containing the canonical representative of $C_0$. Initialize a discovered-code set with that representative and an empty predecessor record.
3. At the beginning of each breadth layer, test every code in the current frontier against the canonical representative of $C_1$. If one matches, follow its stored predecessor records back to $C_0$, reverse the resulting finite list, and return the path with its move certificates.
4. Otherwise, for each code $C$ in the current frontier, call the Reidemeister-neighbor algorithm. For each returned pair $(E,\mu)$, canonicalize $E$ by the finite relabeling procedure in step 1. If its canonical representative has not been discovered, add it to the next frontier and store $(C,\mu)$ as its predecessor record.
5. Replace the current frontier by the next frontier and repeat from step 3. If a layer is empty, continue with empty layers; do not return “inequivalent.”

Code equality in this procedure means equality of canonical representatives under the finite crossing/edge relabelings of the normalized code convention. Every loop in one layer is finite; the number of layers has no fixed bound.

Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. The crossingless one-component code is a separate case: its Gauss data are one empty component word, its DT pairing and crossing-sign vector are empty at $c=0$, and its PD data are the single loop `Loop[1]`; every format also carries an orientation marker, `ccw` or `cw`, for the unit circle $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ in the oriented plane, and the outer-face marker is `outside`. Thus the crossingless code records which direction orients its circle. It has no crossing graph or face-permutation test. Disconnected crossing graphs and disconnected crossingless links are outside this code class.

A **normalized planar-diagram code** with $c>0$ has crossing labels
$C=\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and four dart positions $0,1,2,3$ at each crossing, in
clockwise order beginning with the outgoing over-dart. The opposite pair
$(0,2)$ is over and $(1,3)$ is under. For sign $+1$, the clockwise record is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$; for sign $-1$ it is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$. Edge labels are assigned
by scanning crossings in increasing order and their four dart positions in
order, giving the next positive integer to the pair containing the first
not-yet-labelled dart. The outer face is recorded by its least dart in its
face cycle. These rules remove arbitrary edge-name and face-name choices;
different crossing labelings may still represent the same diagram. At $c=0$
a normalized code is the crossingless record with one of the two orientation
markers above.

A **Gauss code** for an oriented diagram records, in traversal order on each
oriented component, a signed crossing label: $+j$ means the component passes
over at crossing $j$, and $-j$ means it passes under. For a knot there is one
cyclic word; for a link there is one cyclic word per component. Each crossing
label must occur exactly twice in total, once positively and once negatively.
When $c>0$, every listed component word is nonempty; a separate crossingless
component is not part of this code class. The zero-crossing case is only the
one-component code specified above.
The code also carries a separate algebraic crossing-sign vector
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$, one entry for each label. Choosing a basepoint
turns the knot's cyclic word into a based word; changing the basepoint
cyclically shifts the word, and relabeling crossings changes only their names.
The visit order, over/under signs, and crossing-sign vector determine the
crossing rotation system; it is realizable in the sphere only when the
resulting code is spherical. A plane Gauss code also carries an identifier of
one cycle of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

A **signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code**, in this page's convention, encodes a
based oriented knot with $c$ crossings by numbering its $2c$ visits
$1,\ldots,2c$ in traversal order. For each odd visit $2j-1$, record the even
visit $2k$ paired with it as $d_j=+2k$ when the odd visit is over and
$d_j=-2k$ when it is under; also record the algebraic crossing sign
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$ for crossing label $j$, the pair containing odd
visit $2j-1$. Its parity conditions are that
$|d_1|,\ldots,|d_c|$ are exactly the even numbers $2,4,\ldots,2c$, each once,
and each paired crossing has one over-visit and one under-visit. The separate
$\varepsilon_j$ records the crossing sign; signed DT conventions elsewhere
may encode signs differently. The associated cyclic traversal and crossing
signs determine a rotation system, which must pass the same spherical
realizability test. A plane DT code also carries an identifier of one cycle
of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

An **oriented planar-diagram code** labels each edge segment by an integer and
lists its two incident darts at crossing records. Each crossing record lists
its four directed edge ends in clockwise order, beginning with the outgoing
over-dart, and records which opposite pair is over, the orientation of each
strand, and the crossing sign. Every edge label occurs exactly twice, once as
an incoming end and once as an outgoing end. The code must satisfy the local
crossing-order rule above; its crossing graph must be connected when nonempty;
and its rotation system must satisfy $V-E+F=2$. The record also carries an
identifier of one cycle of its face permutation as the outer face. Thus an
arbitrary word in labels, even when each label occurs twice, is not declared
realizable until all incidence, orientation, crossing, connectedness, and
face-count tests pass.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every valid connected one-component
oriented code with a selected outer face, the reconstruction procedure
produces a regular oriented diagram representing that code. Any two such
diagrams with the same code differ only by crossing and edge relabeling and
are planar isotopic. The normalized planar-diagram code of a diagram with $c$
crossings appears among the candidates enumerated at bound $c$. This statement
concerns diagrams and their finite codes; it does not identify distinct codes
that may represent the same knot type. The finite realization and enumeration
claims are choice-free; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is assumed only for the smooth
ambient-isotopy uniqueness clause.

Input a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings,
fixed finite orderings of its arcs and crossings, and an odd prime $p$. The algorithm returns the full set
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$ of assignments of residues in $\mathbb F_p$ to the
arcs satisfying the Fox crossing equations, together with
$|\operatorname{Col}_p(D)|$.

1. Create one variable $x_j$ for each arc in the supplied order, and process
   crossings in the supplied order.
2. At each crossing with overarc $o$ and the two underarcs $i$ and $j$, append
   the homogeneous linear equation $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.
   At a crossing, add the coefficients of any repeated arc in that row.
3. Set the next pivot-row index to $r=1$ and process columns from left to
   right. If $r>c$, mark this and every remaining column free and stop. If
   $r\le c$, search rows $r,\ldots,c$ in order for the first nonzero entry in
   the current column. If none exists, mark this column free and continue
   without changing $r$. Otherwise swap the selected row into row $r$, divide
   row $r$ by its nonzero entry in this column, and add multiples of row $r$
   to every other row to clear this column. Record this column as a pivot
   column with pivot row $r$, then increase $r$ by one. After the scan, every
   column not recorded as a pivot column is free.
4. List the free columns in increasing order and enumerate every tuple in
   $\mathbb F_p^f$ in lexicographic order using the residue representatives
   $0,\ldots,p-1$, where $f$ is the number of free columns. If $f=0$, process
   the empty tuple once. For each tuple, assign its coordinates to the free
   variables. For each pivot row, set its pivot variable equal to the negative
   of the sum of the row's free-column coefficients times those assigned free
   variables. Append the resulting assignment in the supplied arc order.
   Return all appended assignments and their number.

For every odd prime $p$ and every finite regular oriented link diagram $D$,
the algorithm in the Definition terminates and returns exactly
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$. If its reduced system has $f$ free variables, it
returns $p^f$ colorings. It uses at most $a$ pivot steps and at most $ca$
row-entry elimination scans for a diagram with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. A Fox $p$-coloring of a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ assigns an element of $\mathbb F_p$ to each arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing, where $x_o$ is the overarc color and $x_i,x_j$ are the two underarc colors. If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move of type R1, R2, or R3, restriction outside the move disk gives a bijection from the Fox $p$-colorings of $D$ to those of $D'$. Consequently the number of Fox $p$-colorings is unchanged along every finite sequence of such moves. The local bijections use no choice principle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Starting with $U_0$, insert $2N+1$ disjoint type-I kinks, one at a time, to form a diagram $U_N$. Each insertion is one R1 move, so deleting the kinks gives an explicit sequence of $2N+1$ moves from $U_N$ to $U_0$. Both diagrams are regular one-component knot diagrams; their normalized codes are valid and occur among the enumerated candidates at their crossing bounds by [F3] and [F4]. By [A1] and [F9], the finite move sequence makes the represented oriented knots equivalent.

The crossing count difference is $c(U_N)-c(U_0)=2N+1$. By [F1], any single Reidemeister move changes crossing count by at most two. A path of at most $N$ moves could therefore change the crossing count by at most $2N$, so no such path connects these two diagrams. The search through depth $N$ completes its finite layers by [F2] without finding a path, although the diagrams are equivalent by step 1.1. This refutes the statement.

The crossingless unknot has one arc and no crossing equations, so [F5]–[F7] give $3^1=3$ Fox 3-colorings. For the standard trefoil with arcs $x_1,x_2,x_3$, the crossing equations are $2x_1-x_2-x_3=0$, $2x_2-x_3-x_1=0$, and $2x_3-x_1-x_2=0$. In $\mathbb F_3$, $-1=2$, so all rows are $(2,2,2)$; the matrix has rank one and two free variables, giving $3^2=9$ colorings by [F6] and [F7]. These equations do not use strand arrows, so reversing either orientation leaves the count unchanged. If the underlying unoriented knots were ambient-isotopic, orient them compatibly; [A1] and [F9] give a finite oriented move sequence, and [F8] forces the counts to agree, contradicting $3\ne9$. Thus the Fox count is an actual distinction, while a finite failed search alone is not one.
